description:
Scenario: MemoryBackend holds std::sync::Mutex (memory.rs:271) across every backend operation. The await_holding_lock lint is enabled (memory.rs:107) which is correct — no await happens while the guard is held. But the methods themselves are async, meaning a contention spike under any concurrent load (e.g. 100 simultaneous /set calls) will serialize ALL operations on a single mutex AND block the tokio worker thread until each operation finishes (no .await inside, so the worker won't yield).

This is documented (memory.rs:99-104) as 'std::sync::Mutex is used for simplicity'. For a 'reference implementation' that downstream contributors will study, the choice is an attractive nuisance: a contributor copies the pattern into their 'real' backend wrapped around a database connection pool, doesn't realize the lock-holding pattern is testing-grade, and ships a backend that serializes all writes through a single mutex.

Maintenance consequence:
(a) The 'this is reference impl, not production' disclaimer is repeated 4-5 times in module rustdoc but the mutex specifically is called out as 'used for simplicity' — implying it's fine for general use. It is not fine for any production load.
(b) When a contributor's product hits scale, the obvious-from-the-code fix (swap to tokio::sync::Mutex per the rustdoc note) does NOT fix the underlying problem — they still serialize all reads and writes through one lock.

Fix direction: add a 'Concurrency model' bullet to the 'Metadata-specific behaviour' section explicitly stating: 'This impl serializes ALL operations through one std::sync::Mutex. Production backends must use per-account or per-record fine-grained locking or use an ACID storage layer.'
title: MemoryBackend's std::sync::Mutex held during all backend method bodies blocks tokio scheduler — fine for tests, an attractive nuisance under any concurrent load
